the first three lines of your syntax), and gradually add more pieces of
syntax.

Yves.

and you will discover the problem.

Yves.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Help with model identification? Could not compute standard errors!
parts:
On 05/07/2014 07:25 PM, Gabriela Galarza wrote:
> I put so many residual variances because all the environmental observed
> variables are correlated and I want to control for this in the model.

There is no need for doing this. You model these correlations by
postulating a common factor. This factor 'explains' the correlations.

> Still, I excluded the residual covariances among environmental variables
> and got the standard errors.
Good. You have an identified model.
> But the chi-square (p-value) is still zero
You test-statistic is large indeed (compared to the degrees of freedom).
> covariance matrix of latent variables is not positive definite
This is due to the negative variances for DGeo2.
> There is a negative eigenvalue (-0.008117006) (at the end of the page).

That is not a tiny number (tiny would be, -.00000000000001). In any
case, you have a negative variance, and that is usually a symptom of
model misfit.

I am a bit worried about the measurement model for 'DGeo2': do the
indicators have enough in common to 'share' a common factor?

Yves.

messages.author: c1e1212cf2e076c1
messages.subject: Re: Help with model identification? Could not compute standard errors!
parts:
To add to Yves, don't specify so much in your initial model. All those parameters will a) make identification difficult if not impossible, and b) make interpreting the model difficult if not impossible. Start with a very basic hypothesis and move up from there, comparing not only parameters in the equations but also overall model fit.

A couple things that you need to do after you run that first model that converges. Look at the ft indices- how far off is RMSEA from .05, how far from 1 are the CFI etc? That initial chi2 test is mostly useless in my experience (others may have differing opinions). Also run the modification indices to seen where your model can be statistically improved (using theory to decide what changes to make). My bet is you will see that big factor with tons of indicators broken out into smaller factors.

One last thing I noticed you have a very high correlation between two factors. Wen you do the mod indices you will see a ton there and it gets confusing. As a starting point I would focus on the changes related to the indicators in the factors that are so highly correlated. As it stands my bet is you woul have low discriminant validity between those factors.

It would be great if one day someone implemented this approach in R. Then users would not be so much left in the dark on the problem of identification.

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Help with model identification? Could not compute standard errors!
parts:
On 05/08/2014 04:19 PM, Edward Rigdon wrote:
> In the early 1990s, Bekker, Merckens and Wansbeek developed Turbo
> Pascal routines implementing an augmented Jacobian approach to
> evaluating identification.

I have no access to the book (which is out of print), but it should be
relatively straightforward to do this using lavaan (although is not
always clear how the 'Jacobian' is defined).

But for a simple model, you could do something along the lines of:

library(lavaan)
HS.model <- ' visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

# get 'Jacobian' using an internal function
# do not try this at home (the name of the function will change soon)
JAC <- lavaan:::computeDelta(lavmodel=fit@Model)[[1]]

# full rank? ncol(JAC) == 21
qr(JAC)$rank # also 21

So this is an identified model. What happens if we have an
under-identified model:

HS.model <- ' visual =~ x1 + x2 + x3
textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
speed =~ NA*x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

# get 'Jacobian'
JAC <- lavaan:::computeDelta(lavmodel=fit@Model)[[1]]

# full rank? ncol(JAC) == 22
qr(JAC)$rank # 21 (<22)

The rank is 21, while we have 22 free parameters, suggesting that the
model is not identified.

I will investigate this further and perhaps provide a public function
for testing this in the near future.

Yves.
